---
order: 9
unit: challenge
title: "Challenge: repair the report"
summary: "Nib's group audited the school's rubbish and wrote a report, but it is hard to follow. Students repair it with four moves from the course: fix unclear pointing words, choose joining words that do the right job, put the paragraphs in the order the overview promises, and add the explanation a paragraph is missing."
language: maths
node: [AC9E7LA04 n2, AC9E8LA04 n2, AC9E6LA04 n3]
explainPicture: { ref: text.yml#explain-pic, caption: "He could mean Max or Ben, so He is replaced with Ben. As a result says the trip next door happened because of the kick." }
hook: "A report has all the right facts, but readers keep getting lost. Can you fix it without changing a single fact?"
---
Nib's class weighed the rubbish in the school's bins for a week. Their facts are right, but the report is hard to follow. You will repair it in four parts, with four moves from this course: pointing words, joining words, the overview's order, and explaining evidence.

## Predict: what's the problem?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Naming what makes the report hard to follow before fixing it makes students choose the right move for each problem."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "A reader says: 'I kept asking what it meant, some ideas didn't connect, the paragraphs jumped around, and some facts just sat there.' Which moves will fix that?"
  options: ["Clear pointing words, joining words, an order that follows the overview, and explanations", "Longer sentences", "More facts", "A better title"]
  actual: "Clear pointing words fix 'what does it mean', joining words connect the ideas, following the overview fixes the jumping, and explanations stop facts just sitting there. That is the plan for this challenge."
```

## Part 1: fix the pointing words

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Mixing clear and unclear pointing words makes students judge each one, not just trace it."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#links", height: 340 }
hint: ["Trace each dotted word. If it could point to two things, press Not clear.", "After Not clear, choose a fix. Only one fix keeps the facts right: the last sentence says where the food scraps came from."]
smaller:
  check: { type: question, q: "'Our class sorted the rubbish from the canteen bin and the classroom bin. It was mostly food scraps.' Could It be the canteen rubbish? Could it be the classroom rubbish?", options: ["Both could fit, so it isn't clear", "Only the canteen rubbish fits", "Only the classroom rubbish fits"], answer: 0, feedback: [null, "Swap in the classroom rubbish. Does the sentence still work?", "Swap in the canteen rubbish. Does the sentence still work?"], explain: "Both kinds of rubbish fit, so a reader can't tell. That makes It a pointing word to mark Not clear and fix." }
check: { type: board, text: "Trace the clear pointing words. Mark the two unclear ones as Not clear and fix them so the facts stay right.", when: "n_right = 4 and n_wrong = 0 and n_fixed = 2", explain: "We and they (the scraps) are clear. Each It could be the canteen rubbish or the classroom rubbish. The last sentence says the food scraps came from the canteen, so the first It is the canteen rubbish and the paper is the classroom rubbish." }
```

## Part 2: joining words

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Choosing joining words in the report's own context applies the warm-up move inside a real text."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#joins", height: 300 }
hint: ["For each gap, ask how the second idea connects: adds, turns against, result or time?", "Having no paper recycling goes against what you'd expect, so it is a turn."]
check: { type: board, text: "Choose a joining word for each gap.", when: "n_gaps_right = 3", explain: "However turns against the hope that paper is recycled, As a result says what happens because of it, and Also adds the bottles: another thing, not the last step." }
```

## Part 3: put the report in order

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Labelling and reordering the whole report applies the overview's map to a text that has lost it."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#order", height: 450 }
hint: ["Label each paragraph first, then use Move up and Move down.", "The overview says food scraps first, then paper and bottles."]
check: { type: board, text: "Label each paragraph and put the report in the order its overview promises.", when: "n_right = 4 and in_order = 1", explain: "Overview, food scraps, paper and bottles, then a conclusion that pulls them together. The reader now knows where they are at every point." }
```

## Part 4: explain the recommendation

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Adding the missing explanation to the report's key claim finishes the repair with the hardest move."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#explain", height: 320 }
hint: ["Click the example sentence, then press Add a sentence after and type your explanation.", "Say how 23 kilograms of food shows a compost bin would make the biggest difference. Then label it."]
check: { type: board, text: "Add an explanation that says how the evidence supports the claim, and label it.", when: "has_explain = 1 and n_empty = 0", explain: "The claim, the evidence and your explanation now work together: the reader sees why the compost bin comes first." }
```

The board checks that your explanation is there. Read the claim and your explanation together: do they connect?

## Make: repair your own

```step
stage: make
tier: typical
insight: "Running the same four checks on their own longer writing is the course's transfer step."
check: { type: reflect, text: "I took a report or essay of my own and checked four things: every pointing word is clear, each joining word does the right job, the paragraphs follow the introduction's order, and each piece of evidence is explained. I fixed at least one of each that needed it." }
```

```teacher
summary: "The course challenge: students repair a report on a school rubbish
  audit that has the right facts but is hard to follow. They fix unclear
  pointing words, choose joining words, put the paragraphs in the order the
  overview promises, and add a missing explanation, then run the same four
  checks on their own writing."
time: 50
timing: Predict 4 min · Part 1 10 min · Part 2 6 min · Part 3 10 min · Part 4 10
  min · Own writing 10 min
goals:
  - I can find and fix the parts of a text that make it hard to follow.
  - I can choose the right move for each problem.
  - I can run the same checks on my own writing.
struggle: "Part 1 is the hardest: students must decide which pointing words are
  clear before tracing, then choose the fix the facts support. Some will trace
  It to one kind of rubbish confidently. Ask whether the other could fit too,
  then ask which sentence settles it."
before: >
  Try Part 1 yourself: trace We and they, then mark both Its as Not clear and
  choose the fix the last sentence supports.


  The challenge combines four of the course's moves: pointing words (warm-up),
  joining words (warm-up), overviews and order (AC9E7LA04 node 2), and
  substantiation (AC9E8LA04 node 2). Fixing an unclear pointing word by naming
  the thing is the repetition move from Say it again. Word chains and topic
  sentences are not tested here. The rubbish figures are made up for the lesson
  but realistic for a school week. The 10-cent container refund applies in every
  state and territory.


  Students who skipped the warm-up unit may need the reminder in Part 1: a
  pointing word is unclear when two things fit.
running:
  - "Predict: list the three problems on the board. Tick them off as the parts
    are done."
  - "Part 1: ask a student who traced It to the canteen bins to read the
    sentence with the classroom bins swapped in. Does it still work?"
  - "Part 2: name the job before choosing the word."
  - "Part 3: ask which words in the overview decide the order."
  - "Part 4: read three explanations aloud. Which one would convince the
    principal?"
stuck:
  - see: A student traces every pointing word, including the unclear ones.
    ask: Could this point to anything else?
    fix: "If two things fit, it's not clear: name the thing instead, and let the
      other facts decide which."
  - see: A student reorders the report by guessing.
    ask: What does the overview say comes first?
    fix: Follow the overview's order.
  - see: A student's explanation repeats the 23 kilograms.
    ask: Why does that number matter for the compost bin?
    fix: "Say what it shows: food is the biggest part, so composting cuts the most."
stretch: Write the paragraph for the bottle collection recommendation, with a
  claim, evidence and explanation. Then add it to the report in the right place.
support: "The four-check card: Pointing words clear? Joining words right job?
  Order follows the overview? Evidence explained?"
leads: >
  This finishes Holding writing together. The four checks make a good editing
  checklist for any extended writing, in English or other subjects.


  Coming later in How writing works: How sentences work, and Choosing words.
exit:
  q: Name the four checks you used to repair the report.
  a: Pointing words are clear; joining words do the right job; paragraphs follow
    the overview's order; evidence is explained.
explain: >
  A text can have all the right facts and still be hard to follow. Four checks
  fix most of it:


  - Is every **pointing word** clear? If two things fit, name the thing.

  - Does each **joining word** do the right job?

  - Do the paragraphs follow the **overview's** order?

  - Is every piece of **evidence explained**?
class:
  inquiry:
    q: Can a text with all the right facts still be bad writing?
    prompts:
      - What does a reader need besides the facts?
      - Which of the four problems would annoy you most as a reader?
    notes: Yes. Facts need to be connected and ordered so the reader can follow
      them. That connecting is cohesion.
  activities:
    - at: predict
      kind: activity
      title: Read it cold
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Project the unrepaired report (Parts 1 and 2 as they start). Students
        read it once and jot down every place they got lost.
      notes: Collect the spots. Most will be the unclear It and They, which is Part 1.
    - at: make
      kind: discussion
      title: Four checks, your writing
      minutes: 6
      do: >
        Students apply the four checks to a recent piece of their own writing
        and share one fix with a partner.
      notes: This is the transfer the course is aiming at. Keep the four-check card on
        the wall.
  questions:
    - at: end
      title: Which check?
      type: question
      q: A paragraph gives a figure and then moves on without saying what it shows.
        Which check catches it?
      options:
        - Is the evidence explained?
        - Are the pointing words clear?
        - Do the joining words do the right job?
        - Does the order follow the overview?
      answer: 0
      explain: A figure with no explanation is evidence that hasn't been explained.
```

# Texts for "Challenge: repair the report" (cohesion board). Facts written for the lesson.
# [[word>?~a/b]] is an unclear pointing word: the right move is Not clear, then a fix.

# region: links
widget: cohesion
p: [[Our class|class]] sorted the rubbish from the canteen bin and the classroom bin for one week. [[We>class]] weighed every bag. [[It>?~*The canteen rubbish/The classroom rubbish]] was mostly food scraps. [[It>?~*The classroom rubbish/The canteen rubbish]] was mostly paper that could have been recycled. [[The food scraps from the canteen|scraps]] weighed 23 kilograms, and [[they>scraps]] could all have gone into a compost bin.
# endregion

# region: joins
widget: cohesion
p: The classroom bin held 15 kilograms of paper. [[{However|So|First}=However]], our school has no paper recycling. [[{As a result|For example|Meanwhile}=As a result]], all of that paper goes to landfill. [[{Also|But|Then}=Also]], we found 40 drink bottles that could have earned 10 cents each through the container deposit scheme.
# endregion

# region: order
widget: cohesion
mode: parts
layout: blocks
roles: overview body conclusion
tools: order
s overview: This report shows what our school throws away in a week and how we could throw away less. It looks at food scraps first, then paper and bottles.
s body: Most of the canteen rubbish was food scraps, which weighed 23 kilograms in one week. All of it could have been composted.
s body: The classroom bin held 15 kilograms of paper and 40 drink bottles. Paper and bottles can both be recycled.
s conclusion: Food scraps, paper and bottles make up most of our rubbish, and all three could be kept out of landfill. We recommend a compost bin, paper recycling and a bottle collection.
start: 3,4,1,2
# endregion

# region: explain
widget: cohesion
mode: parts
roles: claim example explain
tools: text add
s claim: A compost bin would make the biggest difference to our rubbish.
s example: Food scraps were the heaviest thing in our bins, at 23 kilograms in one week.
# endregion

# region: explain-solution
widget: cohesion
mode: parts
roles: claim example explain
s claim: A compost bin would make the biggest difference to our rubbish.
s example: Food scraps were the heaviest thing in our bins, at 23 kilograms in one week.
s explain: This shows that composting would cut more weight than recycling paper or bottles, because food is the biggest part of what we throw away.
# endregion

# region: explain-pic
widget: cohesion
answer: on
p: [[Max|max]] lent [[Ben|ben]] [[his football|ball]] at lunch. [[He>?~*Ben/Max]] kicked [[it>ball]] over the fence. [[{As a result|However|First}=As a result]], Ben had to knock on the neighbour's door to get the ball back.
# endregion
